summary: Supply the outside diameter, the total rise, the maximum riser rise and the tread angle and the Spiral staircase calculator solves for number of steps. It suits a materials order or a planning estimate you want to get roughly right first time. Change one value and the results step aside until you press Calculate again, which is what makes it easy to see how much the answer really depends on that one input.

sections.title: How does the Spiral staircase calculator work?
sections.html:
The Spiral staircase calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports number of steps in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the outside diameter, the total rise, the maximum riser rise and the tread angle.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Spiral staircase calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Number of steps=rounded up, (total rise ÷ maximum riser rise)
Number of treads=rounded up, (total rise ÷ maximum riser rise) − 1
Actual riser rise=total rise ÷ rounded up, (total rise ÷ maximum riser rise)
Angle of rotation=tread angle × (rounded up, (total rise ÷ maximum riser rise) − 1)
Tread length=-1 ÷ 2 × inside diameter + (1 ÷ 2) × outside diameter
Inside diameter=2 × inner arc ÷ tread angle

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Angle, opening in degrees
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Spiral staircase calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a supplier's figure against your own measurements
  • Quoting a job where areas and quantities drive the price
  • Ordering material and not wanting a second trip
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the outside diameter, the total rise and the maximum riser rise — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Spiral staircase calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns number of steps, derived from the outside diameter, the total rise and the maximum riser rise. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Spiral staircase calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the outside diameter, the total rise, the maximum riser rise and the tread angle, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter inside diameter in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Inside diameter opens in centimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Spiral staircase calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
